source_read: PMC HTML, PMC3475187 (accepted author manuscript): abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results (acute and residual subsections), Tables 1-2 (HTML), Discussion, acknowledgements and declaration of interest read in full; Figures 1 and 2 read on the rendered images (Figures 3-4 legends only).

claims.overstatement: 'Heart rate was still 9-14 beats per minute above placebo' at 24 h implies a persisting drug effect, which this source does not establish: (1) the 24-h values are the baseline of the next-day choice session in an outpatient study, and urine screens did not test for amphetamines (screens were negative 'excluding amphetamines and THC'), so outside use cannot be excluded - the authors themselves flag this; (2) on the rendered Figure 1 the acute-session heart-rate peaks after 12 mg methamphetamine (about 80 bpm) and 50 mg d-amphetamine (about 86 bpm) are lower than the next-day values printed for the same conditions (86.1 and 90.5), which is hard to reconcile with a residual effect of the study dose; (3) the top of the 9-14 range (13.7 bpm) is the 50 mg d-amphetamine condition; for methamphetamine the excess was 9.3 (12 mg) and 11.0 (50 mg) bpm.
claims.note: Supported: plasma peaks 'observed 3-4 h after drug administration' (sampling ended at 240 min; 50 mg methamphetamine plateaued at about 86 ng/ml at 180-240 min and d-amphetamine was still rising at 240 min, so the true peak may be later); cardiovascular peaks within 15 min (holds for heart rate and systolic pressure after 50 mg methamphetamine; after 50 mg d-amphetamine systolic and diastolic pressure peaked at about 90 min in Figure 1). Numbers in the magnitude field match the Residual Effects text: placebo 76.8 (2.3) vs 86.1 (1.9) 12 mg methamphetamine, 87.8 (2.3) 50 mg methamphetamine, 90.5 (3.4) 50 mg d-amphetamine, p<0.01; diastolic 78.4 (2.4) vs 74.4 (2.2) after 50 mg methamphetamine, p<0.05 (values given as mean +/- SEM presumably; not stated). Not supported as worded: the persistence interpretation (see overstatement). Also this study's participants were 13 men described as 'recreational' users (9.4 days/month; 3 with current dependence), outpatients.

anchors.extracted: Both drugs raised plasma levels dose-dependently (p<0.0001); peaks observed 3-4 h after dosing. Blood sampled at baseline, 15, 60, 90, 120, 180 and 240 min only (figure axis shows 30 rather than 15 min). Figure 1: 50 mg methamphetamine about 86 ng/ml at 180-240 min; 50 mg d-amphetamine about 80 at 240 min, still rising; 12 mg doses about 25.

anchors.locator: Results > Cardiovascular Effects > Acute Effects; Figure 1 (rendered)
anchors.extracted: Both 50 mg doses raised heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure vs placebo and vs 12 mg (p<0.01); methamphetamine raised heart rate more than d-amphetamine (p<0.05); peak cardiovascular effects within 15 min. Figure 1: 50 mg methamphetamine heart rate about 91.5 bpm at 15 min vs about 78 after placebo; systolic about 140 at 5 min; d-amphetamine systolic peak about 147 at 90 min.

anchors.locator: Results > Cardiovascular Effects > Residual Effects; Data Analysis; Discussion para 4; Methods > Sample sessions
anchors.extracted: Choice-day baseline (about 24 h after the sample dose): heart rate 76.8 (2.3) placebo vs 86.1 (1.9) 12 mg methamphetamine, 90.5 (3.4) 50 mg d-amphetamine, 87.8 (2.3) 50 mg methamphetamine (p<0.01); 12 mg d-amphetamine not significant; diastolic 78.4 (2.4) vs 74.4 (2.2) after 50 mg methamphetamine (p<0.05). Authors: outpatient setting, possible undetected outside drug use; urine screens excluded amphetamines and THC.

claims.note: Supports dose-related increases in heart rate, blood pressure and positive ratings, and a racing-heart rating at the largest methamphetamine dose ('heart pounding' 66 vs 26, summed scale). Two qualifications relevant to the claim's magnitude field: in this study the 12 mg doses were not reported to raise heart rate or blood pressure significantly (only the 50 mg doses differed from placebo and 12 mg), so 'raised at all doses vs placebo' rests on Hart 2008; and subjective data here are session sums (VAS max 700), not peak 0-100 ratings.

anchors.locator: Results > Subjective Effects > Acute Effects; Table 2
anchors.extracted: Summed VAS (max 700) and DEQ (max 4), placebo / 12 AMPH / 12 MA / 50 AMPH / 50 MA: DEQ good drug effect 0.7 / 0.8 / 1.6* / 2.3* / 3.1* (50 MA > 50 AMPH); stimulated 111 / 160 / 172 / 226* / 320*; heart pounding 26 / 24 / 19 / 29 / 66* (50 MA > all); nose burning raised at 50 mg; tired and sleepy lowered. Both 50 mg doses raised 'good drug effect', 'high' and desire to take again vs placebo and 12 mg.

claims.note: This study supports 'no significant worsening' and the 24-h statement in the magnitude field ('No significant residual performance effects'), and adds divided-attention improvement; but it found no DSST effect at any dose, so the DSST improvement in the claim rests on Hart 2008 alone and this source partly qualifies it.

anchors.locator: Results > Psychomotor Performance Effects > Acute Effects and Residual Effects; Methods > Subjective-Effects and Psychomotor Battery
anchors.extracted: Two tasks only (DSST, divided attention). All active doses of both drugs increased maximum tracking speed; the 12 mg doses shortened mean hit latency (p<0.05); no other significant effects (no DSST effect); no significant residual performance effects about 24 h later. n=13; values only in Figure 4 (change from baseline).

anchors.locator: Results > Psychomotor Performance Effects > Acute Effects
anchors.extracted: DSST not improved at any dose in this study, unlike Hart 2008.

claims.overstatement: 'Almost always chose money when it was $20' overstates the source, which says participants 'overwhelmingly' chose money: on the rendered Figure 2 the $20 group still chose the drug on about 12-22% of the 10 opportunities for active doses (12 mg methamphetamine about 2.2 of 10, 50 mg about 2.0), and the abstract gives 17% drug choices overall under $20 vs 41% under $5. Suggest 'chose money on about 80-90% of opportunities'. Also, $5 and $20 were given to different participants (7 vs 6), so the contrast is between two very small groups and no statistical test of it is reported; the choice also had escalating response costs (50 to 2,800 presses per portion).
claims.note: Supported: 13 men, not seeking treatment; 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine and d-amphetamine chosen on about half of opportunities with $5 (Discussion 47-50%; Figure 2 about 4.7 and 5.0 of 10, both > placebo about 1.9, p<0.05; no difference between drugs); with $20 no significant dose effect. Placebo itself was chosen about 1.9 of 10 times in the $5 group.

anchors.locator: Methods > Participants, Design, Choice (self-administration) sessions; Table 1
anchors.extracted: 13 men (mean age 37.4), current methamphetamine use 9.4 days/month, 3 with current dependence, none treatment-seeking; outpatient; sample day (single intranasal dose 0, 12 or 50 mg/70 kg methamphetamine or d-amphetamine plus $5 for 7 participants or $20 for 6) followed next day by 10 choices between 10% of the dose and 10% of the money, response requirement rising from 50 to 2,800 presses.

anchors.locator: Results > Methamphetamine and d-Amphetamine Choice; Figure 2 (rendered); Discussion para 2
anchors.extracted: $5 group: 50 mg methamphetamine about 5.0 and 50 mg d-amphetamine about 4.7 of 10 choices vs placebo about 1.9 (p<0.05), no drug difference; Discussion: about 47-50% drug choice. $20 group: placebo about 0.4, active doses about 1.2-2.2 of 10, no significant dose effect.

41% vs 17% drug choices under $5 vs $20 (consistent with the means across the four active conditions in Figure 2); authors caution the morning, work-task laboratory setting may not generalize to recreational use.
Choice analysed separately within each money group (single-factor ANOVA by drug condition); no between-group test of $5 vs $20 reported.

key_findings.correction: 'Money was chosen almost always' overstates the source, which says participants 'overwhelmingly' chose money. The rendered Figure 2 shows, in the $20 group, placebo about 0.4 and active conditions about 1.2-2.2 of 10 choices (abstract: 17% drug choices under $20 vs 41% under $5, matching the means of the four active conditions). In the $5 group: placebo about 1.9, 12 mg AMPH 2.9, 12 mg MA 3.7, 50 mg AMPH 4.7*, 50 mg MA 5.0*. Choice counts are therefore readable from the figure.
Rendered Figure 1: 50 mg methamphetamine about 86 ng/ml at 180-240 min; 50 mg d-amphetamine about 80 and still rising at 240 min (last sample), so 'peak 3-4 h' is bounded by the sampling window.

'Peaks within 15 min' (the paper's wording) holds for heart rate and for systolic pressure after 50 mg methamphetamine; on the rendered Figure 1, 50 mg d-amphetamine systolic (about 147 mmHg) and diastolic (about 88) pressure peaked at about 90 min, and diastolic pressure after 50 mg methamphetamine plateaued from 5 to 240 min.

Values confirmed. Add: on the rendered Figure 1 the acute-session heart-rate peaks for 12 mg methamphetamine (about 80 bpm) and 50 mg d-amphetamine (about 86 bpm) are below the next-day values printed for the same conditions (86.1 and 90.5), which argues against a simple residual drug effect and strengthens the outpatient caveat.

reporting_issues.note: Rendered Figure 2 shows asterisks (vs placebo) only on the two 50 mg bars of the $5 panel and no section mark (vs 12 mg).

Resolvable from the rendered Figure 2: no dagger (difference from 50 mg d-amphetamine) or section mark appears on any bar; only the two asterisks. The legend's symbol definitions are generic, and the figure is consistent with the text (no drug difference in choice).

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 high overall for the comparative (methamphetamine vs d-amphetamine) conclusion agreed; within-person dose effects robust.

interpretation_gap.note: The card's own results_show repeats 'money was chosen almost always'; should read 'overwhelmingly' / about 80-90% of opportunities.

missed: Figures 1 and 2 are legible on the rendered images; plasma, cardiovascular and choice values can be read approximately (see corrections).

Next-day heart rate after 12 mg methamphetamine and 50 mg d-amphetamine exceeded the acute peaks for those conditions in Figure 1; together with outpatient status and urine screens that excluded amphetamines, this makes the 24-h heart-rate elevation weak evidence of a residual drug effect. Relevant to cl_meth_pk_intranasal_timecourse, which states it without caveat.
The top of the claim's 9-14 bpm range is the 50 mg d-amphetamine condition (+13.7); for methamphetamine the excess was +9.3 (12 mg) and +11.0 (50 mg).
Minor: the Methods list blood sampling at 15 min, but Figure 1's plasma axis shows 30 min (and labels the axis 'Time (hr)' though the values are minutes).
